Obviously brand name electronics will have a premium padded into their prices just based on the strength of the brand itself but there are also additional things you pay for such as design testing, quality assurance, updates, etc.

If you go by raw hardware specs, brand name products will rarely match up to off-brand ones. However don't expect your new tablet to get a software update when the new OS for it comes out... Also probably not enough people out there use your tablet for some geek to have hacked an open source update and put it on github for you.

I think off-brand stuff is more akin to a lottery. You can get some really nice stuff for really cheap but you're gambling as to whether it breaks, whether you can expand the functionality or whether they have a damn button a few cms too far from your thumb and you have to contort your fingers to use it every time.

Good luck

Yup, it's normally a safer bet to get a brand-name tablet. Granted, it'll cost more up-front but you're much more likely to receive future updates for that model, better testing, etc. If you get lucky with an off-brand tablet and someone has spent the time to keep its software up to date you may be fine for a while as well but depending how obscure it is you may never see an update at all.

The specs are normally going to be in favor of the brand-name models as well. So it's simply going to have more power, look better, etc and would justify future updates from the manufacturer. Whereas some of the no-name brands may have weak hardware that would be almost pointless to continue updating.

Yes and no. With brand name products you typically know what you're getting, but the hype can cloud the actual product quality. With off brand names, you need to do a lot of research to know what you're getting. Including longevity. If it hasn't been around for years, then you just don't know.

The trick is to be able to research well and cut through hype to the core. Personally, I'll start at some of the well known but not flashy brands and work from there.

Im not sure why tablets took off tbh, if you want a decent mobile computer get a gaming laptop. And don't buy Apple unless you like the operating system, it's the same stuff inside but 2-3 times the price of normal not Apple stuff.

Cables are odd, anything that only transmits signal like hdmi or cat5e Ethernet etc. get cheap. USB on the other hand carries a current so slightly more expensive and shorter is better. For example the cable I bought for 9.99 carries about 1500mA/h but a cheapo one I bought only carries 480mA/h (tested myself at work)

Don't buy membrane keyboards either.

Bear in mind to check reviews online because a kickass tv for example might have shifty capacitors (looking at you Samsung) cheap to fix if you know how but an otherwise good tv is dead because of a production fault.

On that note it's better to not buy anything until about a year afterwards when they might have had feedback and had a revision to the manufacturing process, which either means it'll be fixed or you know not to waste your money on it.

Another important aspect to consider when buying an off-brand table is security.

You can get away with generic ones, but you have to know a lot about them. If you're buying a TV or computer monitor, you better know the manufacturer of the panel inside. If you're buying a tablet, you better know all about the CPU and GPU inside. Brand names have a reputation to try and uphold and the other ones don't. Look at people who bought cheap tablets at Fry's and stuff, you could tell if they are going to be slugs by reading the specs and knowing about ARM CPUs. If you don't know about it, research it, and if you don't feel like researching it, then you shouldn't take the risk on generic.

I have a Yamakasi Catleap, a Korean 1440p IPS monitor I bought several years ago for around $300, a good price even by today's standards. I knew going into it, after research, that the actual LCD panel itself was the same one used in more expensive displays, but had potential for defects like dead pixels, color being off, etc. But I researched it and understood the risks, and in my case it was worth it, as it cost a lot less than the 27in Dell Ultrasharp that had the same exact panel. But I had another monitor, so if it was worse than the old one, I would just have used the old one as the primary. I could have mitigated the failure and still made something out of it.

But diving into generic electronics and just reading the advertising materials, box, and product description will usually end with a lot of disappointment. I'd say so much so, that the extra cost of a brand name electronic is worth it if you're not confident in your ability to research online or you're not knowledgeable about the subject being covered.

As you said too, sometimes you need to fix it yourself. So I sort of consider if it's too expensive to replace easily or if I can't or can't fix it. Generic isn't for everyone. If I had a generic tablet and it was slow, I'd put a different ROM on it, one that's more light weight. Obviously not everyone is up to that. It really just depends on how much time you are willing to put into something.

Well, depends, really. The logic I use when buying computer hardware is to buy the mid-high tier hardware or something that costs around 60-70% of the cost of the top of the line of X product. You still get very good support, build quality and a very nice experience overall. This of course comes with exceptions. Then there's the stuff that I flat out refuse to skimp on, such as a good power supply, since the cost of a failing cheap power supply could be an entirely new system. Then there's the stuff that frankly doesn't matter if I choose the cheapest version possible, such as RAM. Soooo, it depends, as I said
